pending_items.title: COP flop triggers backlash in Australia; Pacific nations express despair
pending_items.content:
SYDNEY/ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The finger pointing to assign blame for the collapse of UN climate talks in Turkey began on Monday with calls for the resignation of the Australian minister leading them, while the Pacific island nations most at risk expressed their despair over the failure of countries to collectively address global warming.

For the first time since the 2009 meeting in Copenhagen, the COP climate conference could not reach a final agreement from its talks after the EU and others rejected a final deal that did not include any mention of fossil fuels' role in global warming because of pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing nations.

This was the first meeting since the UN's environmental body confirmed global temperatures were set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) level scientists have said will cause extreme weather impacts to intensify, and the lack of collective action has increased a sense of impotence around the multilateral COP process.

Turkey hosted the latest talks, called COP31, in Antalya but shared leadership with Australia. Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen was the COP31 president of negotiations and opposition politicians in his home country blamed him for the failure.

"This energy minister's got to go because he's a complete and utter failure," Angus Taylor, a member of the Australian parliament who leads the opposition, told reporters on Monday.

"Chris Bowen was responsible for it. He should go," Taylor said.

Speaking after the COP31 talks, Bowen blamed the very strong red lines many parties had on climate change.

Inside the Australian parliament, other opposition members asked Prime Minister Anthony Albanese why he would not sack Bowen after the country had spent A$150 million ($99.23 million) on COP31. Albanese did not comment directly on whether he would ask Bowen to step down.

"We believe that climate change is real. We believe in the science," Albanese said. "Whether it's environmental security or national security, we act in Australia's national interest."

The COP31 talks began on November 9 but the lack of a final agreement extended the summit to a record overtime on Sunday. There was already some contention before their start as Australia, which has been at the forefront of efforts to act against global warming, fought with Turkey over hosting duties.

More than 190 countries were represented, and more than 92,000 people had registered, making it provisionally the largest UN climate conference on record. The United States did not send a delegation.

Last year's talks in Belém, Brazil, produced a deal but no commitment to phase out fossil fuels.

China is the world's biggest emitter of carbon dioxide, the main cause of global warming, and a spokesman for the country's foreign ministry, Guo Jiakun, expressed disappointment at the COP31 outcome during a news conference on Monday but said it "should not lead to a loss of confidence in multilateral process."

Guo added that addressing climate change is a "shared undertaking for humanity" and the global trend toward low-carbon development is "irreversible."

Bhupender Yadav, who led India's delegation at COP31, said India engaged constructively and tirelessly with the presidencies and other parties.

"While concerns remain over certain elements of the cover decision, we remain committed to dialogue and constructive engagement until the very end to build consensus," he said.

Most Pacific island nations, which are facing rising sea levels and other existential threats from climate change, expressed deep disappointment.

"We have been let down on all sides," the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 said in a statement.

Tuvalu, the Pacific island nation that hosted a pre-COP event in October highlighting its exposure to rising sea levels, called out the absence of engagement and transparency in trying to reacha decision on a final statement.

"Listening to parties who diminish the credibility of signs of climate change is disappointing," said Maina Talia, Tuvalu's climate minister, expressing concern about the lack of commitment to put the world back on track for the global temperature goal.

(Addituonal reporting by Peter Hobson and Liz Lee; Writing by Praveen Menon; Editing by Christian Schmollinger)

pending_items.title: إسرائيل: مفاوضات تشكيل الحكومة بين آيزنكوت ونتانياهو تنتهي بدون اتفاق
pending_items.content:
اختتم تكتلا رئيس الوزراء الإسرائيلي المنتهية ولايته بنيامين نتانياهو ومنافسه غادي آيزنكوت، المكلّف تشكيل الحكومة المقبلة، الأحد، جولة جديدة من المشاورات بشأن تشكيل ائتلاف حكومي، من دون إحراز اتفاق، في ظل خلافات تتطلب تنازلات جوهرية من الطرفين.

وبعد حوالى أربع ساعات من المحادثات في فندق في مدينة هرتسليا قرب تل أبيب، اختتم اللقاء بين وفد من حزب "يشار" الذي يتزعمه آيزنكوت وآخر من حزب الليكود بزعامة نتانياهو، وذلك بعد مرور أسبوع على أول لقاء بينهما.

وجاء في بيان مقتضب صدر عن الطرفين في ختام اللقاء أن "مواقف الحزبين بشأن سلسلة من المسائل الجوهرية قُدّمت وشكّلت موضع نقاشات معمّقة".

ولم يعكس البيان الذي اكتفى بالإشارة إلى اجتماع مقبل من دون تحديد موعده أيّ مؤشّرات إلى تقارب محتمل.

وأمام آيزنكوت، رئيس الأركان السابق للجيش الإسرائيلي، مهلة حتى السادس من كانون الأول/ديسمبر، قابلة للتمديد 14 يوما، لتشكيل الحكومة، عقب انتخابات تشريعية جرت أواخر تشرين الأول/أكتوبر، ولم تمنح أيا من الفريقين أغلبية مطلقة.

ورغم امتلاك فريقه 48 مقعدا في الكنيست، من أصل 120 مقعدا، في حين تتطلب الأغلبية المطلقة 61 مقعدا، فإن هذا الفريق لا يزال منقسما بشأن الاستراتيجية الواجب اتباعها لتشكيل ائتلاف حكومي.

وتراوح الخيارات المطروحة بين التحالف مع الأحزاب اليهودية المتشددة دينيا (الحريديم)، أو التقارب مع الأحزاب العربية، أو تشكيل حكومة وحدة وطنية مع حزب الليكود .

اقرأ أيضا مستوطنون إسرائيليون يحرقون ممتلكات فلسطينية في أربع قرى بالضفة الغربية

وكان حزب "يشار" اعتبر السبت إجراء هذه المباحثات "التزاما حقيقيا بتشكيل أوسع حكومة ممكنة"، موضحا أن آيزنكوت طلب من ممثليه بحث جميع الخيارات والاحتمالات المطروحة.

لكن حزب الليكود سرعان ما وضع شروطا عدة لمشاركته في حكومة وحدة وطنية، وهي الصيغة التي يدفع باتجاهها نتانياهو الذي يخوض معركة لضمان مستقبله السياسي.

ويطالب الليكود خصوصا بوقف "جميع الهجمات الشخصية والتحريض على الكراهية" التي تستهدف، بحسب قوله، رئيس الوزراء المنتهية ولايته وحكومته، فضلا عن الالتزام بتشكيل ائتلاف حكومي يضم "جميع الأحزاب التي تؤيد وجود دولة إسرائيل بوصفها الدولة القومية للشعب اليهودي"، مع استبعاد مشاركة الأحزاب العربية.

تواجه الأحزاب العربية التي حققت في الانتخابات إنجازا تاريخيا مع 19 مقعدا، هجمات ممنهجة من نتانياهو وحلفائه، وخصوصا أنها تسعى إلى إزاحته.

ويركز حزب الليكود في محادثاته على عدد من البنود السياسية أبرزها رفض إقامة دولة فلسطينية وإبقاء السيطرة الإسرائيلية في أجزاء من سوريا ولبنان وقطاع غزة، إلى جانب التوصل إلى تسوية في ما يتعلق بتجنيد اليهود المتشددين (الحريديم) وهي قضية بالغة الحساسية في إسرائيل .

ومن السيناريوهات المحتملة، تشكيل حكومة وحدة وطنية تعتمد على التناوب على منصب رئيس الوزراء بين آيزنكوت ونتانياهو، وهي صيغة سبق أن طُبقت في إسرائيل .

وسيوفر اتفاق كهذا لنتانياهو الحصانة السياسية التي تمنحه إياها المناصب الحكومية ولاسيما أنه يواجه تهم فساد .

ويعارض رئيس الوزراء المنتهية ولايته تشكيل لجنة تحقيق مستقلة تتحرى الإخفاقات الأمنية أثناء هجوم حماس على جنوب إسرائيل في السابع من تشرين الأول/أكتوبر 2023.

وكان آيزنكوت ركز في حملته الانتخابية على رفض بقاء نتانياهو في السلطة كما استبعد الانضمام إلى ائتلاف حكومي بقيادته.

اقرأ أيضا إسرائيل: غادي آيزنكوت يدعو حزب بنيامين نتانياهو إلى مفاوضات لتشكيل ائتلاف حاكم

كذلك، جدد نفتالي بينيت، رئيس الوزراء الإسرائيلي السابق السبت، رفضه الانضمام إلى أي ائتلاف مع بنيامين نتانياهو أو تكتله "تحت أي ظروف".

والجمعة، حذر آيزنكوت من أنه لن يسمح بإطالة أمد المفاوضات، مؤكدا أنه في حال عدم إحراز تقدم فيها، فإنه "يعتزم تشكيل حكومة طوارئ وطنية، وسيسعى بعد ذلك إلى توسيعها، سواء قبل أداء اليمين الدستورية في البرلمان أو بعده".

ويمكن أن تحظى حكومة أقلية برئاسة آيزنكوت بدعم خارجي من النواب العرب المنتمين إلى " القائمة العربية الموحدة" (راعم)، و"القائمة المشتركة".

ويعارض القومي أفيغدور ليبرمان حليف آيزنكوت هذا الخيار ويدعو بدلا من ذلك إلى التحالف مع الحزبين الدينيين "شاس" و"يهدوت هتوراة".

pending_items.title: Israeli MP invokes internment of Japanese Americans in call to restrict Palestinian citizens
pending_items.content:
An Israeli MP from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has invoked the mass incarceration of people of Japanese descent in the United States during World War II while discussing how Palestinian citizens of Israel should be treated.

“When the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbour, President Roosevelt signed an order to place all citizens of Japanese descent in internment camps. How is that different from our situation?” newly elected Knesset member Eli Goldschmidt told Channel 14 News on Sunday.

“We are still at war. We have not yet finished dealing with Hamas; we have Arab terrorism in Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank] and problems in southern Lebanon,” Goldschmidt added.

“We cannot allow people who are relatives of those who want to destroy us to be privy to confidential information,” the Likud MP said, referring to Palestinian lawmakers from Ra’am and the Joint List.

Goldschmidt was referring to the controversial executive order signed by US President Franklin D Roosevelt in 1942, which forced the relocation and incarceration of more than 100,000 people of Japanese descent, most of them US citizens.

Palestinian citizens of Israel are descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homeland after the 1948 Nakba, during which Zionist militias expelled around 750,000 Palestinians to establish the State of Israel.

Despite being granted Israeli citizenship, they have long faced discrimination and incitement.

They number around two million, accounting for approximately 20 percent of Israel’s population.

Since the Palestinian-led Ra’am and Joint List parties won a historic 19 seats in the Knesset in last month’s elections, Netanyahu and his allies have led a campaign of incitement against Palestinians in Israel, portraying the two parties as “terrorism supporters” in an effort to prevent the formation of a government reliant on their backing.

Violence against Palestinians inside Israel has since increased. Last week, a mosque in the village of Ed-Dahi, near Afula, was set on fire in a suspected arson attack linked to an Israeli mob.

Later in the interview, Goldschmidt appeared to distance himself from Roosevelt’s executive order, while maintaining that “a democracy at war should prioritise the security consideration”.

“Roosevelt went too far, but the principle of standing firm on security priorities is right for a country in a state of war,” he said .

'It is difficult to comprehend just how far the incitement in Likud has gone, and how it continues to escalate without any restraint'

- Yousef Jabareen, Joint List leader

“I am not recommending that we do what Roosevelt did, but I do suggest not relying on Arab parties in forming a government during wartime.”

Since anti-Netanyahu parties won 67 Knesset seats in the elections, opposition parties, including those led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, have been scrambling to form a new government. However, right-wing parties within the bloc have refused to rely on Ra’am and the Joint List.

Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, condemned Goldschmidt’s remarks, writing in a post on X: “It is difficult to comprehend just how far the incitement in Likud has gone, and how it continues to escalate without any restraint.”

Jabareen said Goldschmidt was “effectively calling for placing all Arab citizens in the country in internment camps”, describing the remarks as “shocking statements”.

“We must not remain silent in the face of this incitement, and above all, they must not remain in power for even one more day. They are an existential threat to all of us,” the Palestinian leader said, referring to the Likud-led government.

pending_items.title: Why is Bangladesh’s Grameen Bank under attack?
pending_items.content:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – When attackers stormed a Grameen Bank branch in Kashiani last week, they did not just damage furniture and equipment. They also destroyed records accumulated over nearly three decades.

Solaiman Morol, the branch manager in Bangladesh’s Gopalganj district, said about a dozen men arrived on the afternoon of November 18 carrying machetes, petrol and tools to break the locks. Staff members were away on field visits.

The attackers looted the branch and tried to cut open its vault with a grinder. They took out about 40 sacks of vouchers and other documents and set them on fire. They also looted steel cupboards, filing cabinets, chairs, tables and other equipment. A staff member’s rice cooker was among the items taken away. “They said that after burning the records, nobody would have to repay their loans,” Morol said.

Videos of the attack later appeared online. Morol said he heard slogans including “Joy Bangla” and “Joy Bangabandhu”, associated with ousted former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina ’s Awami League, as well as calls to burn what the attackers described as “Yunus’s den”.

The branch has not been able to resume normal operations. Staff members have received threats and customers are worried about the safety of their deposits and loan records.

“A bank depends on trust. This is impacting our customers’ confidence. People who have deposits with us are becoming frightened,” Morol said.

The attack was part of a wider wave of violence against Grameen Bank. Its latest internal memorandum, dated November 23, records 97 attacks on branches and offices between November 10 and 23.

The attacks have put the Nobel Prize-winning institution founded by Muhammad Yunus at the centre of Bangladesh’s political tensions, months after he stepped down as chief adviser following Hasina’s removal from power in August 2024. Hasina supporters set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members in Faridpur and Narail.

In a statement on Monday, Yunus called “the systematic assault” on Grameen Bank “unbelievably shocking”, noting that bank officials and borrower-members “narrowly escaped fatal injury” in several incidents.

Grameen Bank is one of Bangladesh’s best-known financial institutions. It pioneered a model of microcredit that provides small loans to people who often cannot access conventional banking services.

About 90 percent of its ownership belongs to its borrower-members, while the government holds the remaining 10 percent. It has around 10.6 million members, most of them rural women, according to its managing director, Sarder Akhter Hamed. Around 5.5 million borrowers have outstanding loans worth more than Tk19,000 crore ($1.53bn). Members also hold deposits of around Tk25,000 crore ($2bn) with the bank.

“There are many people in the communities we serve whom other banks and financial institutions are unwilling to lend to. We stand beside them and provide access to credit,” Hamed said.

The attacks have disrupted the bank’s work and left staff members worried about their safety. Hamed said the institution has around 21,000 employees and that the violence had affected them psychologically. “There is a sense of insecurity,” he said.

The government has blamed the Awami League, the party of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, for the attacks.

“The government is making every effort to maintain law and order,” Ziauddin Ahmed, additional secretary in charge of the political wing at the Ministry of Home Affairs, told Al Jazeera.

The attacks come amid renewed political activity by Hasina’s supporters, which has led to serious unrest in parts of the country, for example Gopalganj, her ancestral district. Hasina supporters have set fire to police stations and the homes of local MPs, and allegedly killed three BNP members.

Political analysts say Grameen Bank has become a symbol through which some Awami League supporters can direct their anger at Yunus, under whose interim rule Hasina’s party was banned from electoral politics. During Yunus’s stint as Bangladesh’s leader, Hasina was also convicted by a tribunal for massacres carried out against protesters who challenged her rule in 2024. Hasina faces a death sentence, but has recently asserted that she intends to return to Bangladesh from India , where she has lived in exile since she was ousted.

Mubashar Hasan, a researcher at the humanitarian and development research initiative at Western Sydney University, said the timing was significant.

“Her party has spent the week pushing for her return. Grameen Bank is the easiest symbol of Dr Yunus they can reach,” he said. “For the Awami League’s hardliners, Yunus is the face of their fall, so burning his bank is a way of hitting back at him.”

The attacks, Hasan argued, may also be intended to demonstrate that the party still has a presence on the streets, despite the ban. “Some of these attacks look like a performance of strength, especially in Gopalganj, to tell supporters ‘we are still here’,” he said.

Asif Mohammad Shahan, a professor in the department of development studies at the University of Dhaka, sees the violence as part of a broader political strategy .

He said the Awami League had two possible routes after the August 2024 uprising: acknowledge its mistakes and seek political rehabilitation, or try to force its way back into politics. In his assessment, the party has chosen the latter.

“The attack on Grameen Bank is actually an effort of sending a message of ‘politics of revenge’,” Shahan said.

He said the attacks could also be intended to provoke the government into a heavy-handed response, allowing the party to portray itself as a victim and challenge the government’s legitimacy.

The bank’s ownership structure makes the attacks especially consequential. Most of its shares belong to the poor women who depend on it for loans, savings and other financial services.

“When a branch burns, it’s their loan files, savings records and repayment schedules going up in smoke,” Hasan of Western Sydney University said.

He warned that disruption could push borrowers towards informal lenders and make it harder for them to continue their repayment cycles.

The damage is already affecting the bank’s operations. Hamed, the Grameen Bank managing director, said the institution had suspended the accrual of interest on outstanding loans at branches unable to operate because of the attacks.

The bank is also trying to protect its staff and property. Some branches have increased security and moved staff from locations considered particularly risky.

But the consequences extend beyond damaged buildings and lost records: At stake is also the confidence of customers in the bank.

The attacks have also raised questions about the ability of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government to maintain law and order.

Ahmed, the Home Ministry official, said “it would be wrong to say that the government is struggling to contain the situation”. Police headquarters told Al Jazeera that eight cases had been filed and eight people arrested in connection with the attacks. “The problem is that our police force is somewhat short of manpower,” Ahmed said.

Shahan said the government’s response was being constrained by the knowledge that a tough crackdown could give the Awami League the chance to play victim. “The Awami League is baiting the government into attacking it so that it can quickly switch to playing the victim and try to delegitimise the government,” he said.

Hamed said police had responded whenever the bank sought help and in some cases had provided advance warnings about possible attacks. “For the most part, however, we have had to remain alert and protect ourselves,” he said.

“If the law-and-order situation in the country improves, confidence and trust [in the bank, too] will automatically return,” he said.

pending_items.title: Bad COP, worse COP: What's next after climate talks fail?
pending_items.content:
The collapse of marathon climate talks in Turkey has renewed questions about reform of their consensus requirement, and galvanised calls for legal action and ambitious side agreements between like-minded countries.

The "conference of the parties" talks, better known as COP31, ended without agreement and two days over schedule on Sunday, as countries deadlocked on fossil fuels, finance, science and carbon-removing technologies.

It was an ignominious end for an unusual dual-presidency shared by Australia and Turkey, and negotiations chair Chris Bowen, who is Australia's climate minister, said it was "very disappointing".

For many observers, the outcome was the inevitable result of a process that has regularly been hamstrung by its insistence on consensus.

"Decision-making that requires every country to agree on every comma is not fit for a climate emergency," said Nikki Reisch, director of the Center of International Environmental Law's climate and energy programme.

"The fundamental root of the problem is that when COP was created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only," he said. "That's a very tough ask."

Sunday's collapse has renewed calls for a reform to that consensus-based process, in which any one country, or a small minority, can nix progress.

"It has been clear for years that the COP process is in need of significant reform," wrote former US vice president Al Gore on X.

He urged a "reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world."

But as Bowen noted, "you also need consensus to change consensus" -- in other words, all countries would have to agree those reforms.

He described that as a "particular challenge," although others might characterise it as simply impossible.

The COP31 talks deadlocked over multiple issues, notably whether the so-called cover decision would mention phasing out planet-warming fossil fuels.

Several countries refused a deal without that mention, while others including Saudi Arabia were vehemently opposed to its inclusion.

There were other serious faultlines, including the timing of scientific work from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and language on carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised by some as costly and ineffective.

Crucially for developing countries, there was also no progress on finance -- the money badly needed to help countries transition energy systems and adapt to the natural disasters climate change is already worsening.

"The fundamental problem for globally agreed climate policy is more starkly obvious than ever: fossil fuel powers will not agree to have their resource wealth devalued, and rich countries won't provide enough climate finance to the developing world," said Frank Jotzo, professor of environmental and climate change economics at the Australian National University.

Other COPs have ended in failure before, including most recently in 2009.

But for all the forum's failings, most agree that the COP process remains important for its unique format, bringing together virtually every country in the world and offering equal billing to all.

As a result, few suggest the process should be abandoned, but there are growing calls for alternatives to advance climate change action, including legal suits.

That route is already being pursued, most notably with an International Court of Justice advisory opinion that confirmed states have a binding legal obligation to combat climate change.

"If the negotiations are not delivering what individual states need, then they'll certainly consider turning to the ICJ and other international courts," said Harj Narulla, an international lawyer who advised the Solomon Islands at COP31.

Others expect growing interest in agreements made outside the COP process, like the Santa Marta initiative, bringing together countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels.

The process grew out of the COP30 meeting in Brazil, where interested nations sought to bypass a lack of consensus on the issue.

Members held talks earlier this year, and agreed some first steps, including an expert scientific panel to advise on pathways.

These "plurilateral processes are growing," said Jotzo, and more are needed, including on carbon removal technologies and finance for adaptation.

Bowen too said he sees the Santa Marta process becoming "increasingly important."

"Doesn't replace COP. It's just another way of doing it," he added.

pending_items.title: Occupied West Bank ‘military zones’ become de facto Israeli settler land
pending_items.content:
Ramallah, Occupied West Bank – Saleh Zahran had a room on his family’s land with a television, a fireplace, a fridge and solar panels. The kids would play in the groves, and the men stayed up late at night watching the stars.

“We’d cook, eat, drink, spend a whole day from morning to sunset,” he says.

Zahran, 39, inherited the farmland, with 120 olive trees, in Deir Abu Mishal, a village west of Ramallah, from his grandfather and father, splitting it among his brothers.

Between 70 and 80 percent of people in the village, which falls in Area B, under joint Israeli-Palestinian control, live off the land, and just a few years ago, there were no settlers nearby.

“We’d come and go whenever we wanted, pick our fruit at our own pace, sell, build, and marry off sons from the olives. Now, it’s all gone,” he told Al Jazeera.

Since settlers set up an outpost in Area B about 1km from his land in June, nobody in his family had been able to reach it. Settlers attacked their cars, and his elderly father was pepper-sprayed while trying to reach the farmland, he says.

On November 10, an Israeli High Court decision granted the village two days of army “coordinated” harvesting, something once unthinkable in Area B.

Zahran set out with his brothers to reach their lands for the first time in five months, but about 20 settlers came at them. They threw stones, smashed the family’s truck and his brother’s four-wheeler and slashed the tyres. He saw no soldiers, and police never arrived despite their calls.

The next day, the army and its liaison office were present. But farmers were held up until about 9am, shown a map of permitted areas, and told to leave by 2:30pm. Ghiyath Nasser, their lawyer, says villagers could reach less than a third of the area in question, so Zahran could harvest only about 20 of his 120 trees.

After five months, Zahran finally reached the farm room that day only to find settlers had stolen or smashed his belongings and were drawing water for their sheep from the two wells he had restored. The saplings he had planted last year had died of thirst.

On paper, it is the settlers who are barred from the Zahran family’s property and the land around Deir Abu Mishal. But in practice, it is Palestinian owners like Zahran who are kept out.

Nasser says that after his first legal petition, the army twice demolished the outpost – which was immediately rebuilt both times – then declared the site a closed military zone for Israelis only. That, Nasser argues, means soldiers cannot demand permits or “coordination” from Palestinian owners – their job is to keep settlers out.

“Sometimes they declare an area closed to settlers, but in the application they close it to Palestinians,” said Wail Qut, a lawyer with the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), who is from Madama, south of Nablus.

Kerem Navot and Peace Now’s July report found that, at the end of 2025, farm outposts effectively controlled more than 1 million dunams (247,105.4 acres), about 18 percent of the West Bank — roughly 750,000 dunams (185,329 acres) taken since late 2022.

In Madama, closures came first, and the outposts followed. Qut says its northern land was never declared a closed military zone, but the effect was the same.

About five years ago, the army gated the road from the village to Nablus, citing security concerns, he says. It was the only access to as much as a third of Madama’s land. The Israeli High Court dismissed the villagers’ petition after the army said farmers could reach the land on foot or by animal and apply for permits.

“It’s a de facto closure, though,” said Qut, with farmers still barred from entering.

Then, last April, an outpost of what Qut estimates are now 10 caravans appeared inside the closed area. He said the army suddenly reopened the gate for the settlers to use. Qut and his brother were stopped by a settler in the same area when they tried to pick olives there this year, forcing them to leave under armed threat.

Dror Etkes, founder of Kerem Navot, which tracks settler land takeovers, says such closures without orders are common across the occupied West Bank. “There is no vacuum in the West Bank,” he said. “Once an area is closed to Palestinian access, settlers sooner or later will come and take it over, and this is exactly what happened in Madama.”

But Qut finds the courts complicit too. When JLAC petitioned over the outpost north of Madama in September, the court gave the state until May 2027 to respond, rather than a few days, as Qut expected.

On November 13, a wedding was due to take place in al-Mughayyir, located at the northeastern edge of the Ramallah governorate. “Despite the pain and the suffering, people rejoice,” said Samir Abu Alia, 60, a village council member whose cousin’s son, Hassan Abu Alia, 30, was the groom. But soldiers violently cut the festivities short.

“The moment the patrols came down, they surrounded the hall, 20 army jeeps, and started throwing stun grenades between the men and the women,” recalled Abu Alia. Soldiers took the groom and relatives away from his bride for two hours. Abu Alia and others say the groom was beaten.

It began earlier that day on the eastern plain, when a settler grazing his flock inside a closed military zone claimed someone from al-Mughayyir had thrown firecrackers or shot at him, although he was unhurt. Soldiers accepted the settler’s claim at face value and then sealed and raided the village. The army quickly targeted the wedding, claiming there were gunshots and firecrackers, which attendees deny.

About 80 percent of al-Mughayyir’s 43,000 dunams (10,625.5 acres) lies beyond its eastern entrance, closed for years. Abu Alia says villagers can now move freely in only about 900 dunams (222.4 acres). “The rest of the land they’ve taken over, they stop people from reaching it, on the pretext of a military zone, on the pretext of security, on the pretext of I don’t know what.”

Here, the outpost came first. Village council member Marzouq Abu Naim says the first outpost on the eastern plain appeared in 2018 and has grown from 200 dunams to 5,000 dunams. He counts a dozen around the village. “One of the settlers comes, brings a tent, pitches it on a hilltop … the second day, the third day, you find there’s facilitation, something not normal: [authorities] run him water, they run him electricity, they lay a road to this tent,” he said.

According to Abu Naim, when villagers tried to use the eastern entrance about two months ago, settlers attacked and tried to burn cars and tractors, and the army did nothing to intervene.

Abu Naim, whose son, Jihad, 32, was shot dead by a settler during an invasion of the village school in April, also lost a 10-dunam grove of about 250 olive trees. “It wasn’t me who planted them, or my father — our grandfathers planted them.”

In August 2025, after a shooting wounded an Israeli teenager, the army ordered olive trees beside a settler road through the plain cleared as a “security threat”, and settlers joined in. Locals say more than 10,000 trees were eventually uprooted, including 230 belonging to Abu Alia.

Documents from the Israeli NGO Yesh Din show the area was closed for 30 days to “preserve the aims of the clearing”. Renewed in October 2025, the order extended to July 2026 with redrawn boundaries, and again through December.

The order bars everyone without a permit, settlers included. But Yesh Din’s legal objection says it is enforced only against the owners, while settlers graze, plough and build on their plots. When the army’s legal adviser declined to enforce the closure against settlers, he referred Yesh Din to the Israeli Defence Ministry’s legal adviser instead, which the NGO says was an effort to absolve the army of responsibility.

Lior Zur, a Yesh Din lawyer representing the petitioners, told Al Jazeera, “Through this policy of selective enforcement, the military turns closure orders into a mechanism for transferring possession of land from its lawful Palestinian owners to settler trespassers.”

The pattern runs across the West Bank. In March, a closed zone around Duma was enforced against Israeli solidarity activists protecting Bedouin families, rather than settlers; after soldiers removed the activists, settlers invaded the encampment, forcibly displacing the community the next day.

In Burin , farmland sits in closed zones renewed every month or two; settlers have gutted five greenhouses in these closed zones already. In Taybeh , an August order barred Israelis and foreigners, but settlers and outposts remained, including one near the edge of Area B that led to another unevenly enforced closed zone.

Similar cases have occurred in Ein al-Duyuk , Qusra , Umm al-Khair and elsewhere. In closed and firing zones the Israeli army has not used for decades, Etkes said, settlers are “filling in”, even though the orders formally apply to settlers, too.

The result, this olive harvest season, has been unprecedented levels of violence and access restrictions. The United Nations Humanitarian Country Team for the occupied Palestinian territory said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks that caused casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season. The infrequent “coordination” access windows, it said, are often followed by “cancellations, denial of entry, expulsion or attacks”.

“What started as local initiative has been adopted by the military and is today, maybe not a declared policy, but an implemented policy,” said Etkes. The outposts are “not legal, but they are completely supported by the military, by the government, without officialising it”. The Israeli Civil Administration has leased large areas of the West Bank to settlers for grazing, which they never do for Palestinians, Qut said.

“Military closed-zone orders and settler takeovers of Palestinian land are two complementary practices,” said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for Israeli NGO B’Tselem. “The military uses these orders to drive Palestinians off their land, while settlers are frequently allowed to remain or establish outposts.”

Back in Deir Abu Mishal, olives are rotting on trees as the season ends. Zahran’s three young children ask why they cannot return to the farm room for barbecues and the olive harvest. He tells them it is too dangerous. “Four or five settlers stop a whole village, 5,000-6,000 people, from going to the land,” Zahran said. “We are living the height of injustice.”

pending_items.title: Saudi Arabia's influence loomed large over failed COP31 deal
pending_items.content:
By Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane

ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 23 (Reuters) - As the COP31 climate conference drifted into what proved to be record overtime, a negotiator from a small island state complained that a promised meeting with the talks' Turkish and Australian presidents had been cancelled yet again.

Saudi officials, meanwhile, had regular access, allowing them disproportionate influence at the Antalya conference, according to negotiators from Europe, small island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa.

Riyadh was at the forefront of resisting language on reducing reliance on fossil fuels, the negotiators said, adding that was chiefly why a political agreement could not be reached for the first time since 2009.

The European Union, several small island states, and othernations particularly vulnerable to climate change said they could not accept a text that failed to mention the oil, gas, and coal that scientists say drive global warming.

"This COP, I believe, was hijacked by some oil states," Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien told Reuters on behalf of the European Union when asked about Saudi Arabia's role in the negotiations.

The Turkish COP presidency said in a statement no group or country was given "preferential treatment". Representatives for Saudi Arabia and Australia did not immediately comment for this story.

Saudi Arabia and fellow members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries have long opposed climate language targeting fossil fuels, saying they need to be part of the global energy mix for the foreseeable future.

Fossil fuels were explicitly mentioned in texts from previous COPs in 2021 in Glasgow and 2023 in Dubai.

But several negotiators said Riyadh's hand was strengthened at Antalya by the absence of active US engagement at COP31 and the lack of close US-China coordination that has helped broker compromises at previous COPs.

"Instead of having one or two major players helping define the boundaries of the discussion, those boundaries have become less clear," Singapore Environment Minister Grace Fu said.

COP31 began with modest expectations. Host Turkey was pushing a pledge to boost global electrification, and promising to emphasize implementation of past climate deals meant to help the planet avoid the worst consequences of global warming.

But divisions deepened after the Turkish presidency released a revised draft cover text that omitted any reference to fossil fuels.

As countries spent the second week of the talks trying to forge consensus around the wide range of options, delegates and observers said Saudi Arabia kept a fixed position: the text must not mention fossil fuels, and it should include language boosting carbon capture technologies that can reduce their emissions.

One delegate from an Asian country involved in the talks said Riyadh framed the positions as non-negotiable, even existential.

Saudi Arabia was not the only side unwilling to compromise, however. The European Union also hardened its position.

When asked how talks were going on Saturday, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said: "It's either going to be a good deal or it's going to be no deal."

Germany convened meetings with small island states and other members of the High Ambition Coalition, which groups vulnerable nations, African countries and developed countries, including Singapore and Canada.

Together they produced a letter, backed by around 130 countries, that said any deal at Antalya must include mention of transitioning away from fossil fuels, and sent it to the presidency.

Around the same time, and as Saturday slipped into Sunday, Saudi, Chinese and Russian officials frequently visited the presidency's offices, even as representatives from other groups struggled to get meetings, delegates told Reuters.

AN ANGRY REACTION TO SUNDAY'S COLLAPSE

When the revised text finally emerged early on Sunday, many countries reacted angrily. The text largely ignored the coalition letter: it still had no mention of fossil fuels and kept strong language promoting carbon capture.

"It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis," Maina Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, said at the time.

As Sunday wore on, negotiators openly discussed the possibility that the talks could collapse without achieving a political statement. Delegates were leaving Antalya to catch flights. Time was running out.

After the closing plenary started on Sunday afternoon in Antalya, COP31 president Murat Kurum said he could see there was no agreement and confirmed he would not advance any new text.

Some negotiators were left with the feeling the producers of the fossil fuels that have contributed to climate change wielded more power than those who want to accelerate the transition to a low-carbon world.

"It seems like when fossil fuels cannot be mentioned in the cover text, then somehow the oil countries have a larger voice at this COP," said Danish Climate Minister Samira Nawa.

pending_items.title: لبنان: توقيف ثلاثة أشخاص ضبط بحوزتهم 264 كيلوغراما من المتفجرات
pending_items.content:
أعلن الجيش اللبناني، الأحد، توقيف ثلاثة أشخاص يُشتبه بتورطهم في تهريب أكثر من 260 كيلوغراماً من المواد المتفجرة من سوريا إلى لبنان، بعدما ضبط الشحنة في شرق البلاد، وذلك بعد مرور أكثر من شهر على ضبط شحنة مماثلة تعود إلى حزب الله .

وذكر الجيش ، في بيان، أنه "نتيجة عمليات الرصد والمراقبة للحدود الشمالية والشرقية" ضبط في عملية جرت السبت في شرق لبنان "حوالى 264 كلغ من المواد المتفجرة (حوالى 203 كلغ من مادة C4 و61 كلغ من مادة TNT) المهرَّبة من الداخل السوري".

وقال إنه أوقف ثلاثة أشخاص "مشتبه بتورطهم في تهريبها"، مضيفا أن القضاء باشر التحقيق مع الموقوفين.

وأفاد مصدر أمني لبناني لوكالة الأنباء الفرنسية بأن شحنة المتفجرات هربت إلى لبنان من سوريا عبر "مناطق وعرة ونقطة غير شرعية".

وقال إن "الأشخاص الثلاثة الذين أوقفوا هم مهربون مدنيون وغير حزبيين"، مضيفا أن التحقيقات ستظهر من هي "الجهة التي استقدمت لها هذه المتفجرات".

ويأتي ذلك وسط ضغوط متزايدة على حزب الله المدعوم من طهران لتسليم سلاحه، بعدما أضعفته حربان متلاحقتان مع إسرائيل منذ العام 2023. وأقرّت الحكومة اللبنانية بعد الحرب التي انتهت بوقف لإطلاق النار في تشرين الثاني/نوفمبر 2024، واحتلت إسرائيل خلالها مساحات من جنوب لبنان، خطة لنزع سلاح الحزب.

وسبق أن ضبطت الأجهزة الأمنية اللبنانية في تشرين الأول/أكتوبر شاحنة محملة بمواد متفجرة أثناء نقلها من شرق لبنان نحو بيروت، وأوقفت شخصين كانا بداخلها. وأقر الحزب بأن الشاحنة تعود له، وكانت تنقل "قدرات تستخدمها المقاومة في مقاومة الاحتلال الإسرائيلي".

كما أعلن الجيش اللبناني في تشرين الثاني/نوفمبر مداهمة مستودع في ضاحية بيروت الجنوبية، معقل الحزب، ومصادرة كمية من الأسلحة وتوقيف شخص، دون أن يذكر الجهة التي تمتلك المستودع.

وفي 18 تشرين الثاني/نوفمبر، ادعى القضاء اللبناني على خمسة أشخاص ينتمون إلى حزب الله بتهمة "تأليف مجموعة مسلحة" بعد توقيفهم في منطقة بعيدة عن المعاقل التقليدية للحزب وفق ما أفاد مصدر قضائي.

وقال مسؤول العلاقات الاعلامية في حزب الله ، يوسف الزين، الأسبوع الماضي، لصحافيين بينهم مراسلة وكالة الأنباء الفرنسية، إن "واحدا من الموقوفين الخمسة في صفوف حزب الله، لم يكن في مهمة حزبية عند توقيفهم".

اقرأ أيضا حزب الله يقر بأن شحنة متفجرات صادرتها السلطات اللبنانية تعود له

وانتقد النائب عن الحزب حسين الحاج حسن في تصريح نشره إعلام حزب الله، الجمعة، توقيف الرجال الخمسة "بشكل تعسفي، ومن دون أي مسوغ قانوني، رغم أنهم لم يكونوا في أي وضع مشبوه، ولم يكن في حوزتهم أي سلاح أو مواد غير قانونية".

واعتبر أن "هذا الادعاء المرفوض والمدان" يشكّل "مسارا خطيرا ويضع السلطة وبعض الأجهزة الأمنية والقضائية أمام المساءلة حول خلفيات هذه الممارسات وأهدافها، ومدى خضوعها للضغوط والتدخلات الخارجية".

لعرض هذا المحتوى من اليوتيوب من الضروري السماح بجمع نسب المشاهدة وإعلانات اليوتيوب.

يبدو أن إحدى التطبيقات الموجودة في متصفح الإنترنت الذي تستخدمه تمنع تحميل مشغل الفيديو. لتتمكن من مشاهدة هذا المحتوى، يجب عليك إلغاء استخدامه.

وأجرت الحكومتان اللبنانية والإسرائيلية في الأشهر الماضية مفاوضات مباشرة برعاية أمريكية، نتج عنها اتفاق إطار في حزيران/يونيو نصّ خصوصا على نزع سلاح الحزب وانسحاب إسرائيل تدريجيا من مناطق تحتلها في جنوب لبنان، وانتشار الجيش اللبناني بدءا من مناطق "تجريبية".

ويرفض الحزب المفاوضات المباشرة مع إسرائيل ونتائجها، كما نزع سلاحه.

وتعهد الرئيس اللبناني جوزاف عون في كلمة، السبت، مواصلة العمل على حصر السلاح بيد الدولة.

وقال: "انتهى زمن السلاح خارج الدولة"، معتبرا أنه "أدى واجبه في حقبة سابقة"، ومشيرا في الوقت ذاته إلى أنّه حمّل لبنان "خسائر باهظة... حين بات علنا، أنه في خدمة قضايا غير لبنانية".

pending_items.title: Analysis-Can climate diplomacy build on the collapse of COP31?
pending_items.content:
By Peter Hobson, Simon Jessop, Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane

ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 23 (Reuters) - The collapse of COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change.

For the small, vulnerable countries most exposed to rising sea levels and the increasingly extreme weather scientists link to rising carbon emissions, annual UN conferences are their chance to draw the world's attention to their plight and seek financial help.

But the failure of the Turkish talks, which follows on from weak outcomes at other COPs in recent years, lays bare the need for change.

Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, director of environment in Peru's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said "the credibility of the process" was at stake.

"This system needs in-depth reforms," he said.

Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief representing the UN convention that underpins international climate talks, said the consensus-based system can still function, but work was needed.

"I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here," he said as the talks ended on Sunday.

THREE DECADES OF SEEKING A GLOBAL SOLUTION

Two stand-out victories for UN climate diplomacy were the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, when the world for the first time agreed on legally binding targets to curb climate emissions and the 2015 Paris agreement, which established an aspiration to limit global warming to no more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).

A major difference in Paris compared with Antalya was that the US was still engaged in the climate process in 2015.

The Antalya talks, the first since a UN report saying the world was set to breach the 1.5 C threshold that can prevent the worst consequences of warming, marked the second climate conference since US President Donald Trump withdrew from the UN climate process.

China, the world's biggest carbon emitter, but also a major part of the solution as a provider of low-carbon technology, has attended the talks but sought to be low profile.

James Fletcher, who led the CARICOM group of Caribbean nations in Antalya, cited the lack of a major power backing a positive outcome as a big issue.

"There isn't that one party that has sufficient gravitas that can get parties that may be far apart to come together," he said.

Delegates said, however, the need for a multilateral deal to direct the shift towards renewable energy has become less necessary as renewable energy becomes economically compelling.

China's clean energy exports last year alone, for example, will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year once deployed —an amount equal to the emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the ​Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The business world as a result is less dependent on COPs to guide investment decisions.

"It used to be that you'd worry about how these (COP) decisions might affect the investment signal," said Chris Dodwell, co-head of the sustainability centre at Impax Asset Management.

"I don't think they really have that impact anymore …. the economics have taken over and are driving the transition."

And bad as the absence of a deal was, some saw a hint of the positive in the wider refusal to accept a weak deal.

The determination of big oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia, to block language on fossil fuel, arguably reflected the scale of progress that has been achieved.

"The fact that they are blocking so much is also an expression of the fact that we are accelerating the transition," Mattias Frumerie, Sweden's chief negotiator, said.

"They're seeing the direction of travel and this is the forum where they can express their frustration."

Like-minded governments, meanwhile, have focused on smaller groups to get things done. They have formed alliances to push together for faster emissions cuts and to rally finance, forestry initiatives, and efficiency programmes.

Such forums include the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, or TAFF, the Green Grids Initiative, the Global Methane Pledge and the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance.

"There is growing interest in how can we work together to move, not through consensus, but through a coalition of people that are willing to work together," said Maina Talia, climate minister of Tuvalu, which will next year host TAFF. As one of the low-lying Pacific island nations, Tuvalu is particularly keen for rapid action to address climate change.

He said he expected roughly 90 countries to send representatives including Britain, Mexico and Nigeria.

Fiji, another Pacific island, voiced its exasperation with COP.

"It is exhausting and frustrating and disappointing when you come year in, year out and there is no movement," Lynda Tabuya, Fiji's climate minister, said.

The country's chief negotiator, Sivendra Michael, however, said the consensus-driven process of COPs remained vital to ensuring the progress achieved by previous conferences was maintained.

"I do not know how else we are going to bring together all the parties that have committed legally to a legally binding agreement, hold up to their commitments, and discuss how they implement these commitments," he said.

(Reporting by Peter Hobson, Simon Jessop, Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane; editing by Barbara Lewis)

pending_items.title: Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands
pending_items.content:
Guatemala has circulated a proposal to member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) that closely echoed demands made by the United States and Israel to severely restrict the court's powers, Middle East Eye can reveal.

The three-page paper was submitted at a closed-door retreat for ambassadors from ICC member states in The Hague on 18 November, less than two weeks before the court's Assembly of States Parties (ASP) opens its annual session.

The proposal advocated for dialogue with the US over curbing the ICC's ability to pursue cases involving nationals of countries that aren't members of the court, such as the US, Israel and Russia.

MEE understands that Washington's G7 allies, including the UK, Germany and Italy, expressed a readiness to discuss the proposal with the US but were reluctant to advocate the idea publicly.

As a result, Guatemala, a Latin American country allied with Israel and the US, decided to take the lead and draft the proposal.

The document, seen by MEE, reflects Washington's longstanding opposition to the prosecution of Israeli leaders and the court's ability to also prosecute US officials for crimes committed on the territory of member states.

The paper floats requiring consent from a suspect's country of nationality even when the alleged crimes took place on the territory of an ICC member state.

It also calls for an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on immunity and advances arguments that echo Israel's challenge to the way the ICC prosecutor handled the Palestine investigation.

The proposal also says Washington's views should be taken into account in discussions about the court's governance because the US hosts assembly sessions in New York.

This year's session, which begins 30 November, was moved to The Hague amid concerns that US sanctions and visa restrictions could limit participation.

The assembly president and secretariat are expected to draft a resolution regarding Guatemala’s proposal and to circulate it to member states for negotiation, sources told MEE.

MEE reached out to Guatemala, the UK, Canada, Italy, Germany, Japan, France and the ASP for comment.

MEE understands that France appeared to be the only country in the group willing to consider talks aimed at protecting the court from efforts to weaken its jurisdiction.

The UK foreign office declined to comment on discussions between state parties prior to the ASP. A source reiterated that the UK supports "constructive and inclusive dialogue" with non-member states.

The initiative came after Washington imposed far-reaching sanctions on the court in October while granting the court a six-month grace period to take measures that would address US demands.

Once fully in effect in April, the sanctions could stop the court from transacting in US dollars and potentially cripple its operations.

Earlier sanctions had already targeted half the court's judges, and all top prosecutors under an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in February 2025 to penalise the officials for their work on the Palestine and Afghanistan investigations.

The idea of dialogue with the US was a key topic in last year's Assembly of States Parties in December after an EU diplomat presented the US demands for discussion. The US made those demands as a condition for lifting sanctions.

MEE revealed at the time that member states disagreed on what a dialogue would entail, and by the end of the conference agreed that any talks should aim at ensuring the independence and effectiveness of the court.

'The one thing that cannot be part of a dialogue in the face of a treaty negotiation is the jurisdictional provisions of the Rome Statute'

- Kimberly Prost, Canadian ICC judge

The Guatemalan proposal is consistent with MEE's previous reporting on US demands, including the fact that Washington had pressed the court to drop its investigations into Palestine and Afghanistan and urged member states to amend the Rome Statute to bar prosecutions of nationals of countries outside the court.

The US and Israel, non-members of the ICC, have both rejected the court's jurisdiction over their nationals.

Territorial jurisdiction is a foundational principle of the ICC since its establishment in 2002.

The Rome Statute, its founding treaty, allows the ICC to prosecute genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed on the territory of a member state, regardless of the suspect’s nationality.

That provision allowed the court to investigate alleged crimes by US personnel in Afghanistan and provided the basis for arrest warrants issued in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes in Gaza.

Palestine has been a member of the court since 2015.

In a controversial decision earlier this month, ICC judges ordered the closure of the court's Afghanistan investigation that covered alleged war crimes by US forces, despite ongoing attempts by prosecutors to appeal the decision.

Instead, they lauched a new inquiry focused solely on alleged crimes by the Taliban, the de facto Afghan government.

The move raised questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies.

Trump's executive order has allowed the US to sanction those who help the ICC investigate or prosecute certain individuals without their home country’s consent.

In an apparent alignment with the US, the Guatemalan paper recommends making consent from a suspect's country an additional requirement even where the court already has jurisdiction on territorial grounds.

It also proposes asking the ICJ, the UN's highest court, for an advisory opinion on Article 98, a controversial provision in the Statute which addresses whether immunity can prevent a country from handing a foreign official over to the ICC.

The paper also echoes Israel's unsuccessful bid to have the ICC give it another chance to investigate its own crimes in Gaza domestically.

Under the court's rules, known as "complimentarity," countries have the first chance to investigate and prosecute alleged crimes. The ICC can step in if the accused country is unwilling or unable to do so genuinely.

The ICC opened its investigation into alleged crimes in Palestine in March 2021 and formally notified Israel that year.

Israel later argued that the events of 7 October 2023 and a new request by seven member states to launch additional investigations had changed the scope of the investigation and that prosecutors should have notified it again.

This notice explains what the investigation will cover and gives the concerned state a chance to argue that it is already investigating the same matters itself, a principle designed to stop duplication.

Judges rejected Israel's arguments in November 2024, and appeals judges upheld that decision in December 2025.

The appeals judges, however, are still examining Israel's separate challenge to the court's jurisdiction in the Palestine situation.

Kimberly Prost, a Canadian ICC judge who was part of Canada's delegation at the 1998 conference that negotiated the Rome Statute, told MEE that territorial jurisdiction was "at the heart of the Rome Statute".

"You can have a dialogue with the US. I believe in diplomacy. I believe in discussions," she said during a briefing with journalists on Thursday at the ICC.

But said she had told diplomats there had to be "clear red lines" in talks with Washington and called for "strong measures" alongside statements and diplomacy.

Prost was not commenting on any particular proposal. She was responding to a question by MEE regarding a Dutch report claiming the Netherlands was involved in dialogue with the US over the demands. The Dutch foreign ministry has dismissed the report as inaccurate.

Prost was a member of the 2020 appeals chamber that authorised the Afghanistan investigation , which could cover alleged crimes by US personnel. She was sanctioned by the US last summer over that role.

She is one of three ICC judges who have sued the Trump administration over the sanctions .

"There may be things that could be done under the rules. Maybe we need some clarification on legal points that could go to the ICJ or wherever. But the one thing that cannot be part of a dialogue in the face of a treaty negotiation is the jurisdictional provisions of the Rome Statute," she said.

"You can't just change that because a group of states decide that it's inconvenient at this point in time," she added.
